title: Merino Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Merino wells have a median depth of 80 feet, with local drilling costs shaped by shallow plains geology and water-use requirements.
h1: What Merino, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Well records within five miles of Merino show a generally shallow, productive groundwater area, but the records also have limits. The median reported depth is 80 feet, and 94% of reported pump yields are above 15 gallons per minute. That is useful local context when buying land, but it is not a guarantee for one parcel.

Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with some alluvial and Ogallala wells. Before closing, compare nearby well permits, confirm the permitted use, and have a driller evaluate access, casing, grout, pump sizing, and the proposed well location.

sections.heading: Merino well depths are usually shallow
sections.html:
Merino-area wells have a median reported depth of 80 feet. The middle half runs from 63 to 100 feet, so a driller working from nearby records may initially price a relatively shallow hole. Still, the deepest record reaches 480 feet, and 6% of wells fall between 300 and 600 feet.

Depth is influenced by the exact ground under the lot, the target water-bearing zone, casing and grout requirements, and the intended use. Records show 69% of wells under 100 feet and 25% between 100 and 300 feet. For a bid, use local records as a planning range rather than treating the median as a guaranteed stopping point.

sections.heading: Reported yields are strong, but verify the well
sections.html:
Among the 196 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half stretches from 15.0 to 1200.0 gallons per minute, and 94% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 1% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while none report under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures are encouraging for a Merino buyer, but they describe reported tests, not a promise for an unbuilt well. Ask for the neighboring well’s completion report and pumping information. A domestic permit still controls legal use, and an exempt household-use well is subject to Colorado rules, including the 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Merino water levels look stable in the records
sections.html:
The 43 wells reporting static water levels show a median depth to water of 16 feet. The middle half is from 10 to 23 feet below the surface. That suggests a relatively shallow water level for many sites, which can reduce pumping lift compared with a much deeper water table.

The decade comparison does not show a documented drop: the median static water level is 16 feet in both the 2010s and the 2020s. This is not a full groundwater study. Static levels depend on season, recent pumping, measurement method, and location. Have the driller check nearby records and measure an existing well before relying on the data for a new building plan.

sections.heading: Long permit history, with several local drillers
sections.html:
Merino has a long well-permit record, with permits issued from the 1950s through the 2020s and the newest permit year listed as 2026. The busiest decade in the records was the 2000s, with 183 permits. The use mix is mainly domestic or household at 43%, stock at 27%, and irrigation at 28%; monitoring accounts for 8%.

The most active named drillers are Canfield, Leslie George, with 113 records; Stewart Drilling Co., Stewart, Dennis W., with 91; and Canfield Drilling Company, Canfield, Harold E., with 55. Older records may not reflect current availability or pricing. Treat these names as useful permit-history leads, then confirm who is licensed and working locally now.

sections.heading: What a Merino well may cost to drill
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $35 to $55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $2,800 to $4,400. That is only the drilling portion.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,800 to $16,400 at the median depth. The final bid can move with access, casing and grout, pump size, rock or difficult formations, trench length, electrical work, and whether the hole must go deeper. Ask for separate line items and clarify what happens if the well is dry or does not meet the intended use.

sections.heading: Checks before buying near Atwood or Merino
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main pattern in the reported Merino data, but an individual parcel can still produce a poor well or require a deeper hole. The aquifer labels also deserve attention: 887 records name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, while 14 are alluvial and 9 identify the Ogallala. Fractured formations can vary sharply over short distances.

Within about 10 miles, mapped environmental information includes 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, with no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Check the exact parcel, test existing water for bacteria, nitrate, and site-relevant contaminants, and keep the well separated from septic components as required. Confirm the permit, legal use, access for drilling, and building-site layout before excavating.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Merino, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Merino is 80 feet. The middle half runs from 63 to 100 feet, and 69% are under 100 feet. Depth is not uniform: the deepest record is 480 feet, so nearby permits should guide the estimate for a particular lot.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Merino?
faq.a: The local model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,800 to $4,400. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,800 to $16,400. Access, casing, grout, formation conditions, and final depth can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Merino wells produce?
faq.a: Of the 196 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 94% above 15 gallons per minute and no reported wells under 1 gallon per minute. These are reported results, not a guarantee. Request a neighboring completion report and a proper test for the parcel.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Merino, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit record alone. There are 3 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, so check the exact location and test existing or new water. Also test for common well-water concerns such as bacteria and nitrate, and inspect the wellhead and septic layout.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Merino?
faq.a: The available reported static water levels do not show a change by decade. The median depth to water is 16 feet in both the 2010s and the 2020s, with the overall middle half from 10 to 23 feet. Only 43 wells report static levels, so this is a local permit-record indicator, not a complete groundwater trend study.
